stem: An older adult takes twelve medications prescribed by several clinicians. Which concern should the nurse prioritize during medication review?

options.A: Review the complete regimen—including prescriptions from all clinicians, OTC products, vitamins and supplements—for adverse effects, interactions, duplication, ongoing need, and medication-management problems.
options.B: Review only medications prescribed by the admitting clinician because drugs from other prescribers are outside the current medication review.
options.C: Stop the oldest medications first because duration of therapy is the primary criterion for deprescribing in polypharmacy.
options.D: Assume the regimen is safe when every drug was prescribed by a licensed clinician, even when several prescribers are involved.

rationale: The National Institute on Aging notes that older adults often take many medicines, which increases the risk of side effects, drug interactions, duplicate ingredients, and medication-management difficulties. NIA advises patients and clinicians to maintain and review a complete list that includes prescriptions from all prescribers, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, dietary supplements, and herbal remedies, and to ask whether every medicine is still needed. Therefore A is correct. B creates an incomplete reconciliation, C uses medication age rather than clinical indication/risk as the deprescribing criterion, and D incorrectly assumes multiple valid prescriptions cannot interact or duplicate therapy.
educational_objective: Perform comprehensive medication review in older adults with polypharmacy by reconciling all prescription, OTC and supplement products and assessing ongoing need, interactions, adverse effects, duplication and medication-management burden.
source_document_title: Taking Medicines Safely as You Age
source_version_date: Current NIA medication-safety guidance live-rechecked August 16, 2026
source_locator: Medication safety sections: tell providers about all medicines including those prescribed by other doctors, OTC drugs, vitamins, supplements and herbal remedies; mixing products can cause serious problems. Keeping track: maintain a complete list. Do I need to take so many medications?: polypharmacy is a concern in older adults and taking many medications increases side-effect and unintended-problem risk; discuss whether any can safely be reduced/stopped.
source_claim_supported: Older-adult polypharmacy requires comprehensive review of all prescription and nonprescription products for interactions, side effects, duplication, ongoing necessity and management problems rather than assuming safety because each medication was individually prescribed.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: perform medication reconciliation, identify adverse effects/interactions/duplication, monitor medication response, and provide safe medication teaching across transitions of care.
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — older-adult polypharmacy and comprehensive medication review

source_original.rationale: The National Institute on Aging identifies polypharmacy as a particular concern in older adults. Taking many medicines can increase the risk of adverse reactions, drug interactions, and medication-management difficulties, making comprehensive review important.
source_original.source_detail: Polypharmacy/medication management: maintain and review a complete list because multiple medicines increase adverse-effect and interaction risk. Live NIA page currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: medication administration, adverse effects/interactions, monitoring, reconciliation and teaching. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the polypharmacy construct and key A, expanded the comprehensive review to include prescriptions from all clinicians, OTC/vitamins/supplements, ongoing need and duplicate-ingredient/management risks, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium because the final item tests a defined comprehensive medication-reconciliation principle.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current NIA/NIH medication-safety guidance; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: NIA Taking Medicines Safely as You Age live-rechecked 2026-08-16
audit_findings.exact_locator: NIA sections on all medicines/supplements, keeping a medication list, interactions and polypharmacy/deprescribing
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item appropriately prioritizes comprehensive reconciliation and risk/need assessment without instructing the nurse to independently stop medications or use medication age as a deprescribing rule.

distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because incomplete reconciliation can miss interactions, duplication and products from other prescribers.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because deprescribing is based on appropriateness/need/risk, not simply which drug is oldest.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because multiple legitimately prescribed products can still interact, duplicate ingredients or create adverse effects/management problems.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A describes a comprehensive, safety-focused review of the entire medication regimen.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are medication-review strategies for the same polypharmacy scenario.
audit_findings.blueprint: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — medication reconciliation, interaction/adverse-effect assessment and safe management.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked current NIA medication-safety/polypharmacy guidance, all alternatives, rationale, objective, ambiguity, cueing and NCSBN mapping. A remained uniquely correct.
